title: Container With Most Water
summary: You get a list `height` of n non-negative integers: a vertical wall of height `height[i]` stands at position i. Any pair of walls makes a tank. Water between them rises only to the shorter of the two, and it spans the distance between their positions, so the tank holds (shorter height) × (distance) units. The walls in between don't block anything. Return the most water any pair of walls can hold.

examples.explanation: The walls at positions 1 and 5 hold min(9, 8) × 4 = 32. The two outer walls are farther apart, but the 1 at the right end caps them at 1 × 6 = 6.
The short walls in between don't matter: the two 6s hold 6 × 4 = 24.

approaches.twist: Move the pointer at the shorter wall inward, keeping the best area seen so far.
Try every pair of walls and keep the largest amount of water.
approaches.note: Works, but checking every pair takes O(n²) time, about 5·10⁹ pairs for 10⁵ walls. The target is O(n).

signals.meaning: The answer is a pair. Instead of trying all O(n²) pairs, start with the widest one, the two outer walls, and move inward: each step rules out one wall for good.
The shorter wall caps the water. Paired with any wall closer in, it still caps the level while the width shrinks, so it can't do better: move its pointer inward and keep the taller wall.
Width counts, so the two outer walls make the widest tank. Each move inward gives up width, which only pays off if it reaches a taller wall.

constraintReading: len(height) can reach 10⁵, so trying every pair means about 5·10⁹ area checks: O(n²) is far too slow. Aim for O(n), one inward pass that rules out a wall at each step. Only two indexes and the best area are stored, so the space is O(1).

related.relation: Same inward pointers, but a sum compared with a target decides which one moves; here the pointer at the shorter wall always moves.
